sq.q: Explain how a stack is used internally to implement recursion. Illustrate your answer by describing the stack behavior during the evaluation of a recursive factorial function fact(n).
answer: Recursion is a programming technique where a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem. Each recursive call must eventually reach a base case, which is the condition to stop further calls.
Every time a recursive function is called:
A stack frame is created and pushed onto the call stack .
This frame contains information like: The value of the argument (n) The point in the program to return to after the function finishes
The point in the program to return to after the function finishes
When the base case is reached:
The system starts popping frames off the stack , calculating and returning results back to the previous calls
This is known as stack unwinding .

lq.q: You are tasked with transferring 3 delicate data disks from Server A (source) to Server C (destination), using Server B (auxiliary) for temporary storage. Only one disk can be moved at a time, and a larger disk cannot be placed on top of a smaller one. Describe how this real-world data transfer problem maps to the Tower of Hanoi recursive algorithm. Write the recursive steps to solve this for 3 disks, and explain how the function call stack represents each move.
answer: Tower of Hanoi is a mathematical game or puzzle that consists of three rods also called pegs and N number of disks of various diameters. These disks are arranged in ascending order from the top, the smallest at the top, thus approximating a conical shape. This puzzle is shifting all the given N number of disks from the source peg to the destination peg with the help of an alternate or auxiliary peg.
The game consists of three pegs and several disks of different sizes, which can slide onto any peg.
The disks are initially placed on one peg in order of decreasing size so that the smallest disk is at the top and the largest disk is at the bottom.

The objective of the game is to move the entire stack to another peg, obeying the following rules: Only one disk can be moved at a time. Each move consists of taking the upper disk from one of the stacks and placing it on top of another stack or an empty peg. No disk may be placed on top of a smaller disk.
Only one disk can be moved at a time.
Each move consists of taking the upper disk from one of the stacks and placing it on top of another stack or an empty peg.
No disk may be placed on top of a smaller disk.
The puzzle can be solved in the minimum number of moves, which is (2^n)-1, where n is the number of disks.
These rules apply to any version of the Tower of Hanoi puzzle, regardless of the number of pegs or disks used.
void towerOfHanoi(int n, char source, char destination, char auxiliary)
// Base case: If there's only one disk, move it directly
printf("Move disk 1 from %c to %c\n", source, destination);
// Step 1: Move n-1 disks from source to auxiliary
// Step 2: Move the nth disk from source to destination
printf("Move disk %d from %c to %c\n", n, source, destination);
// Step 3: Move n-1 disks from auxiliary to destination
printf("Tower of Hanoi solution for %d disks:\n", n);
towerOfHanoi(n, 'A', 'C', 'B'); // A = Source, B = Auxiliary, C = Destination
Moving 3 disks from A to C via B
When n = 3, source = A, destination = C, auxilliary = B,
Disk 3 from C to B → Disk 2 and 3 Placed at B.
Disk 1 from A to C → Disk 1 Placed at C.
